lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 1.

items.signText:
EARLY DEPARTURES
Breakfast in the restaurant starts at 7.00. If you are leaving before then, please order a packed breakfast at reception before 10 pm the night before. You can collect it from reception from 5.30 a.m.
items.question: What should guests do if they need breakfast before 7.00?
options: a) Go to reception at 10 p.m. to have something to eat.
b) Collect a packed breakfast from the restaurant at 5.30.
c) Ask at reception for a packed breakfast the evening before.
items.explanation: The notice says 'please order a packed breakfast at reception before 10 pm the night before'. The breakfast is collected from reception, not from the restaurant, and 10 pm is the latest time to order, not a time to eat.

items.signText:
Dear Mr Price,
Thank you for your booking. Unfortunately, the sea-view room you asked for is not available on your first night. We can give you a room at the back that night and move you into a sea-view room the next day, at no extra cost. Please let us know if this is acceptable.
Harbour Hotel
items.question: Why has the hotel written to Mr Price?
options: a) To ask him to agree to a change for one night.
b) To offer him a cheaper room for his whole stay.
c) To tell him that his booking has been cancelled.
items.explanation: The sea-view room is 'not available on your first night', so the hotel offers another room that night and asks him to 'let us know if this is acceptable'. The change is only for the first night, the price stays the same ('at no extra cost'), and the booking is not cancelled.

items.signText: Sam – the tourist office has no tickets left for Saturday's boat trip. There are still a few for Sunday at 10, but it finishes at 1, which is after our train leaves. Do you want me to book them and change the train, or shall we forget the trip? Let me know by 5. Mia
items.question: What does Mia want Sam to do?
options: a) Tell her whether she should book the Sunday trip.
b) Go to the tourist office before 5 o'clock.
c) Change their train tickets to a later time on Sunday.
items.explanation: Mia asks 'Do you want me to book them and change the train, or shall we forget the trip? Let me know by 5.' She wants Sam's decision. She offers to change the train herself, so Sam does not have to do it, and nobody needs to go to the office by 5 – that is only when she needs an answer.

items.signText:
FREE CITY WALKING TOURS
Tours leave from outside this office every day at 10.30 and 14.30. There is no need to book – just turn up. Our guides are always grateful for tips. Groups of more than ten people, please contact us in advance.
items.question: What does the notice say about the walking tours?
options: a) Visitors have to pay the guide at the end.
b) Large groups should arrange their tour beforehand.
c) Everyone must book a place at the office the day before.
items.explanation: 'Groups of more than ten people, please contact us in advance' means big groups should arrange it beforehand. The notice says 'There is no need to book – just turn up', and the tours are free: tips are welcome but not required.

items.signText:
SWIMMING POOL
Open daily 7.00–21.00.
Children under 12 must be with an adult at all times.
The pool will be closed on Thursday morning for cleaning, but the gym will stay open as usual.
items.question: What does the sign say?
options: a) Children are not allowed in the pool on Thursday.
b) The gym is closed on Thursday morning.
c) Young children cannot swim without an adult.
items.explanation: The sign says 'Children under 12 must be with an adult at all times.' On Thursday morning the pool is closed for everyone, not only children, and it is open again later; the gym 'will stay open as usual'.

questions.question: Lucy and her husband want a beach holiday with their two children, aged four and six. They want a beach where it is safe for small children to swim, and they would like to cook their own meals. They also need something for the children to do indoors if it rains.
questions.explanation: Sandy Bay has a beach 'where the water stays shallow a long way out' with lifeguards, 'every caravan has its own kitchen', and 'if the weather turns bad, the indoor play centre offers games, crafts and films for under-tens'. The Hilltop Hotel also has a beach 'perfect for young children', but 'rooms do not have kitchens' and its kids' club is outdoors.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Tom wants a quiet holiday away from traffic, where he can spend his days walking in the hills. He is also interested in history and would like to find out about the people who have lived in the area.
questions.explanation: On the Isle of Carra 'no cars are allowed', 'paths lead over the hills', and the museum 'tells the story of the families who have lived here for over a thousand years'. Glenmore Lakes also has walking paths, but it is 'next to the main road' and says nothing about history.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Priya and her friend are students with very little money. They enjoy going out to hear live music at night, and they would like to learn how to cook some local food during their holiday.
questions.explanation: In Valmora the bars and squares 'fill with live music until the early hours', a hostel bed 'costs just £15 a night', and at the Kitchen School 'local chefs show small groups how to make the region's famous dishes'. Brenton Harbour Hostel is also cheap and has a cookery class, but it warns 'don't expect much nightlife'.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Mr and Mrs Gordon are retired and do not want to drive on holiday. They would like to stay in a comfortable hotel where they can relax in a spa, and they want to go out on the water to see wildlife.
questions.explanation: The Seacliff Hotel has 'comfortable rooms' and a spa, 'guests do not need a car' because a free minibus meets every train, and 'boat trips leave twice a day to watch the dolphins and seals'. The Hilltop Hotel also has a spa, but 'guests will need a car' and it offers no boat trips.
options: A
B
C
D
E
F
G
H

questions.question: Daniel has never tried water sports before and would like to have lessons in sailing or windsurfing. He wants to go camping and take his dog with him.
questions.explanation: Windy Point Campsite gives 'sailing and windsurfing lessons for complete beginners', you can 'pitch your tent', and 'dogs are very welcome'. Glenmore Lakes is also a campsite with boats, but only 'experienced sailors can hire boats', 'we do not offer lessons' and 'we cannot accept pets'.
options: A

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 3.
lesenParts.text:
Wildlife photographer Emma Hartley talks about her work.

People often imagine that my job involves travelling to beautiful places and taking amazing pictures every day. The truth is rather different. I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days – and on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with.

I became interested in wildlife when I was about ten. My grandfather lent me his old camera, and I used to sit in his garden trying to photograph the birds at the feeder. Most of the pictures were terrible, but I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long. I didn't think of photography as a career, though. At university I studied biology, and I planned to become a scientist.

Everything changed during my final year, when I joined a research trip to Scotland to count sea birds. I took my camera along just for fun, but one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine. To my surprise, they printed three of them. That was when I realised that I could combine my two interests.

The first few years weren't easy. I earned very little and had to work in a camera shop at weekends to pay the rent. But the job taught me a lot about equipment, and I met photographers who gave me useful advice.

Nowadays I work mainly for magazines and conservation organisations. Before a trip, I spend weeks reading about the animal I want to photograph: where it feeds, when it is most active and how it reacts to people. Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera. Last spring, for example, I wanted to photograph otters in Norway. Local fishermen told me the otters came out at dawn, so I was in my hiding place by four o'clock every morning. On the sixth day, a mother and two young otters appeared just metres away.

The part of the job I find hardest is not the cold or the early mornings but being away from my family. My son is seven now, and I try not to accept jobs that last more than two weeks.

Young people often ask me how to start. My answer is always the same: begin close to home. You don't need to travel to Africa. A local park is full of wildlife if you are patient enough to look for it. And remember that the animal always comes first. If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.

questions.question: What does Emma say about her job in the first paragraph?
questions.explanation: Emma says 'I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days'. She says 'the truth is rather different' from what people imagine, so it is not as exciting as people think, and 'on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with', so good photos are not easy to get.
options: a) It is as exciting as most people think.
b) It is easy to get good photos on most trips.
c) She usually knows exactly when the animals will appear.
d) Most of her time is spent waiting.

questions.question: What did Emma enjoy about photographing birds as a child?
questions.explanation: She says 'I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long'. Her photos were not good ('Most of the pictures were terrible'), and the text does not mention showing them to her grandfather or learning bird names.
options: a) Seeing how good her photos were.
b) Learning the names of different garden birds.
c) Having to be patient and silent for a long time.
d) Showing her pictures to her grandfather in his garden.

questions.question: How did Emma's career as a photographer begin?
questions.explanation: On the research trip 'one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine', which printed three of them. She went to Scotland 'to count sea birds', not to work for a magazine, and she took her camera 'just for fun'.
options: a) A scientist sent some of her photos to a magazine.
b) She went to Scotland to take photos for a magazine.
c) Her university teachers told her to study photography.
d) A magazine offered her a job when she finished university.

questions.question: What does Emma think about preparing for a trip?
questions.explanation: She reads about where the animal feeds and when it is active, and says 'Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera.' The fishermen in Norway are only one example, and seeing the otters 'on the sixth day' does not mean she limits her trips to six days.
options: a) Knowing about the animal is more important than having good equipment.
b) She must ask local fishermen for advice before every trip.
c) She needs to buy a more expensive camera for each new animal.
d) She should never plan to stay in one place for more than six days.

questions.question: What advice would Emma give to a young person who wants to photograph wildlife?
questions.explanation: Emma tells young people to 'begin close to home' because 'a local park is full of wildlife', and says 'If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.' She says 'You don't need to travel to Africa', and earlier that an expensive camera matters less than preparation.
options: a) "Buy the best camera you can afford before you start."
b) "Practise near where you live, and never upset the animals."
c) "Get as close as you can to an animal, even if it seems nervous."
d) "Save up so that you can travel to places like Africa."

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 4.
lesenParts.text:
Most parents have had the same experience. They knock on their teenager's bedroom door at nine o'clock on a Saturday morning. There is no answer. It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy. (1) ______

During the teenage years, the body's internal 'clock' changes. This clock controls our daily pattern of sleeping and waking. The brain starts producing melatonin, the chemical that makes us feel sleepy, around two hours later than it did in childhood. (2) ______ But school still starts at the same time, so the alarm goes off long before their bodies are ready to wake up.

Sleep matters at every age, but it is especially important for teenagers. Experts say teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. Surveys show that most of them get fewer than seven. (3) ______ Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate in class and to remember what they have learnt. They are also more likely to feel anxious or low. They catch colds more often, too. Their results in sport can suffer as well.

Phones make the problem worse. Many teenagers take them to bed and message friends or watch videos until late. (4) ______ The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime, so melatonin arrives even later.

So what can teenagers do? There are some simple answers. Sleep experts suggest going to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends, and leaving phones in another room. (5) ______ Some schools in the UK and the USA have even started lessons an hour later, and teachers there say that students are more awake and get better marks. Perhaps other schools will soon follow their example.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (1)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before says 'It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy.' 'However' contrasts with this idea, and 'a much better explanation' introduces the next paragraph, which explains the body clock. The sentence about online time cannot go here because phones have not been mentioned yet.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (2)?
questions.explanation: 'In other words' repeats the idea that melatonin arrives 'two hours later' in simpler words. The next sentence, 'But school still starts at the same time', contrasts with 'not ready for sleep until much later', and 'their bodies' is repeated in 'before their bodies are ready to wake up'. The sentence saying teenagers 'sleep much longer' contradicts the article.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (3)?
questions.explanation: 'The difference' refers to 'between eight and ten hours' needed and 'fewer than seven' actually slept. 'A serious effect' is then explained by the list that follows: students find it harder to concentrate, feel anxious and catch colds. The sentence saying teachers 'did not notice any difference' contradicts these effects.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (4)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before describes teenagers who 'message friends or watch videos until late' – the time they spend online. The gap sentence says this is not the only problem, and the next sentence gives the second problem with 'also': 'The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime.' The sentence about morning light cannot go here because 'help too' needs an earlier piece of advice.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

questions.question: Which sentence best fits gap (5)?
questions.explanation: The sentence before gives two pieces of advice from sleep experts, and 'can help too' adds a third. The next sentence, 'Some schools ... have even started lessons an hour later', adds one more solution. The sentence saying 'none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement' cannot go here: it refers to 'this' before the later start has been mentioned, and it contradicts the teachers, who say students 'get better marks'.
options: A) In other words, their bodies are simply not ready for sleep until much later in the evening.
B) It is not just the time they spend online that matters, however.
C) Their teachers, however, did not notice any difference at all.
D) However, scientists now believe that there is a much better explanation.
E) Because of this, teenagers today sleep much longer than their grandparents did.
F) Getting outside in the morning light can help too, because it resets the body clock.
G) The difference may not sound very big, but it can have a serious effect.
H) Sadly, none of the schools that tried this saw any improvement.

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 5.
lesenParts.text:
Last April I ran my first marathon through the streets of my home city. I had (1) ______ up running two years earlier because I wanted to get fit, but at the beginning I couldn't run for more than ten minutes (2) ______ stopping. It was a friend from work who finally (3) ______ me to enter the race.

I found a training plan online and (4) ______ my distance a little every week. I trained three times a week, in the rain, in the dark and sometimes even in the snow. By the end, some of my long runs were taking more than three hours.

On the day of the race, the (5) ______ was amazing. Thousands of people stood along the streets, clapping and shouting our names, and bands were playing music on almost every corner. By kilometre 35 my legs were really hurting and I wanted to stop, but the crowd kept me going.

I crossed the finish line in four hours and ten minutes. I was completely exhausted, but I have never felt so (6) ______ of myself. I've already signed up for next year's race.

questions.question: Gap (1): I had ____ up running two years earlier because I wanted to get fit.
questions.explanation: 'Take up' means to start a new hobby or activity: 'I had taken up running'. 'Get up' means to leave your bed, 'put up' means to build or raise something, and 'make up' means to invent – none of them mean starting a sport.
options: a) got
b) put
c) taken
d) made

questions.question: Gap (2): I couldn't run for more than ten minutes ____ stopping.
questions.explanation: 'Without stopping' means continuously, with no break. 'Unless' must be followed by a clause (unless I stopped), 'instead' needs 'of' (instead of stopping), and 'except stopping' does not make sense here.
options: a) instead
b) without
c) except
d) unless

questions.question: Gap (3): It was a friend from work who finally ____ me to enter the race.
questions.explanation: Only 'persuade' is followed by object + to-infinitive: 'persuaded me to enter'. We say 'suggested that I enter', and 'made' and 'let' are followed by the infinitive without 'to' (made me enter, let me enter).
options: a) persuaded
b) suggested
c) made
d) let

questions.question: Gap (4): I found a training plan online and ____ my distance a little every week.
questions.explanation: 'Increase' takes an object and means to make something bigger: 'increased my distance'. 'Grow' and 'rise' do not take an object here (my distance rose), and 'add' needs 'to' (added to my distance).
options: a) grew
b) rose
c) added
d) increased

questions.question: Gap (5): On the day of the race, the ____ was amazing.
questions.explanation: 'Atmosphere' is the feeling created by the people in a place, and the next sentence describes it: people 'clapping and shouting our names' and bands playing. 'Climate' is the usual weather of a region over many years, 'surface' is the top of the road, and 'nature' means plants and animals – none of these are described.
options: a) atmosphere
b) climate
c) surface
d) nature

questions.question: Gap (6): I was completely exhausted, but I have never felt so ____ of myself.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'proud of yourself'. 'Pleased' and 'happy' are followed by 'with' (pleased with myself), and 'glad' is not used with 'of myself'.
options: a) glad
b) proud
c) pleased
d) happy

lesenParts.instruction: Read the text(s) and answer the questions in Part 6.
lesenParts.text:
When I was a child, I always wanted to learn the guitar, but my parents couldn't afford lessons. Two years ago, on my fortieth birthday, I finally bought one and tried to teach (1) ______ by watching videos online.

The beginning was hard. My fingers hurt quite (2) ______ lot, and they weren't strong (3) ______ to press the strings down properly. After a month I nearly gave (4) ______ playing.

Then my daughter found me a teacher, Sara, and everything changed. She explained that the pain happens to all beginners and that the skin gets harder with practice. Apart (5) ______ the technique, she has taught me to read music and to play in a band with other adult learners, which is the best part of my week.

I now try to practise for twenty minutes every evening (6) ______ I am working late. Next month our music school is having a concert, and I am going to play in front of an audience for the first time. I'm nervous, but also very excited.

questions.question: Gap (1): I finally bought one and tried to teach ____ by watching videos online.
questions.explanation: The subject 'I' is also the person who learns, so the verb 'teach' needs the reflexive pronoun 'myself' ('teach myself' = learn without a teacher). 'Me' is not correct when the object is the same person as the subject.

questions.question: Gap (2): My fingers hurt quite ____ lot.
questions.explanation: 'Quite a lot' is a fixed expression meaning 'very much'. 'Lot' needs the article 'a' here; 'quite the lot' or 'quite lot' are not correct.

questions.question: Gap (3): They weren't strong ____ to press the strings down properly.
questions.explanation: 'Adjective + enough + to-infinitive' says whether something has the necessary quality: the fingers did not have the strength needed. 'Enough' comes after the adjective ('strong enough'); 'too' and 'very' go before it.

questions.question: Gap (4): After a month I nearly gave ____ playing.
questions.explanation: 'Give up + -ing' is a phrasal verb meaning 'stop doing something'. The writer found it hard and almost stopped. 'Gave in' is not followed by an -ing form, and 'gave away' needs an object like 'the guitar'.

questions.question: Gap (5): Apart ____ the technique, she has taught me to read music and to play in a band.
questions.explanation: 'Apart from' means 'as well as / in addition to'. 'Apart' is always followed by 'from' in this expression.

questions.question: Gap (6): I now try to practise for twenty minutes every evening ____ I am working late.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'except if': the writer practises every evening, but not on the evenings when they work late. 'If' or 'when' would mean the opposite (practising only on those late evenings).

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
horenParts.transcript:
Man: Excuse me, I'm here for the Year 10 parents' evening. Is it in the library, like last term?
Woman: Not this time, I'm afraid. The library's being painted this week. We'd planned to use the dining room, but it's too small for all the teachers' tables, so everyone's in the main hall. Just go down this corridor and it's the double doors on your left.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

Girl: Dad, Mrs Palmer says everyone in the orchestra has to take something to the concert tomorrow evening.
Man: Not your music stand again? It's still in the car from last time.
Girl: No, the school's got plenty of those now. And they've borrowed chairs from the church hall, so we don't need to bring our own. It's the lights, actually. The hall will be quite dark while we're playing, so we all need a small torch to read our music.
Man: I think there's one in the kitchen drawer. I'll check the batteries.

Girl: Are you going to be in the talent show, Josh? I thought you might play your guitar.
Boy: I did think about it, but loads of people are doing music. And I'm definitely not dancing. You've seen me try!
Girl: So what are you going to do, then?
Boy: I've been writing some funny stories about school life. I'm going to stand up on stage and tell jokes. Mr Grant says it's fine as long as I'm kind about the teachers.
Girl: That'll be brilliant.

Girl: Guess what, Gran? I came first in the school art competition!
Woman: Oh, well done, love! What did you get? Last year the winner got a big box of paints, didn't they?
Girl: They did, but I've already got loads of paints. This year the winner got a ticket for the new exhibition at the city gallery, and I can take someone with me. The girl who came second got a book of famous paintings.
Woman: That sounds lovely. So who are you taking?
Girl: You, of course!

Boy: Did you hear about the Year 9 trip? We were supposed to be going to the castle, but Mr Hughes says the coach company can't do that date.
Girl: So is it cancelled?
Boy: No, they've changed it. We're going to the science museum in the city instead, because the train goes straight there. Some people wanted the farm park, but that's closed until the spring.
Girl: Oh well, the museum's got that new space exhibition, so I don't mind.

Woman: Hello, this is a message for all parents from Kingsmead School. Sports day is going ahead this Friday, but please note that the start time has changed. The races were going to begin at half past ten, but because very hot weather is forecast for the afternoon, the first races will now start at quarter past nine. Students should arrive at school at nine o'clock as usual, wearing their PE kit, and bring a bottle of water. Thank you.

Woman: You're not playing computer games already, are you? What about your homework?
Boy: I've done the maths worksheet. I finished it at lunchtime. And the science poster isn't due until next Friday.
Woman: So there's nothing else?
Boy: Well, there's the history essay. Mr Dean wants it on his desk first thing tomorrow morning, and I've only written the introduction.
Woman: Then the games can wait, can't they?

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 2.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: So you've started your engineering course. What's it like?
Man: It's hard work. The lectures are long, but the lecturers make them really interesting. What I love most, though, is the time in the workshop. Last week we built a small bridge and tested how much weight it could take. That's why I chose engineering, really.
Woman: And it's four years, isn't it? That seems a long time.
Man: It goes quickly when you enjoy it.

Girl: I heard you're giving up your job at the café. Is it the money?
Boy: No, the pay's actually quite good for a weekend job, and Sue, the manager, is lovely. It's just that my exams start in May, and at the moment I'm working every Saturday and Sunday. I've got so much revision to do that something has to go.
Girl: Will they let you come back in the summer?
Boy: Sue says they will, so that's good.

Man: So, what do you think of the new office, now we've been here a week?
Woman: I was worried it'd be really noisy with everyone in one big room, but actually it's been fine. And because the design team sit right next to us now, I can just turn round and ask them things instead of sending emails. We've sorted out more problems this week than in the whole of last month.
Man: The journey's worse for me, though. It's a much longer walk from the station.
Woman: Oh, it's about the same for me.

Woman: Have you got a minute, Mr Clarke?
Man: Of course, Helen. If it's about your holiday dates, I've already said yes.
Woman: Thanks, but it's not that. I heard that Tom's team is behind with the new website. I've finished all my own work for this month, so I wondered if I could join them for a couple of weeks.
Man: That would be a big help, actually. Tom will be delighted.

Boy: How was the interview for the summer job at the museum?
Girl: They kept me waiting for twenty minutes, which wasn't ideal, but I didn't really mind because it gave me time to calm down. And then it went better than I expected. I'd read all about the museum beforehand, so I could answer all their questions, and they even laughed at my joke about the dinosaurs!
Boy: It sounds like you'll get it.
Girl: Well, I really think I've got a good chance.

Woman: How's your online Spanish course going?
Man: Well, I'm not sure about the teacher. She talks really fast and she doesn't always explain the grammar.
Woman: I've found that with mine too. But for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain, can you? The evening class at the college costs four times that.
Man: That's true. You get a lot for the price. And the lessons are only forty minutes, which suits me.
Woman: Me too. I couldn't concentrate for any longer after work.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 3.
horenParts.transcript:
Woman: Good morning, everyone. I'm Kate Morris, the manager of the new Riverside Sports Centre, and I'd like to tell you what we're offering when we open next month. The opening day is Saturday the twelfth of March. We were hoping to open in February, but the builders needed a little more time to finish everything.

The centre has a twenty-five-metre swimming pool, a sports hall and a gym. But the thing we're proudest of is our climbing wall, which is the tallest in the region. Beginners are very welcome. You don't need any experience, because an instructor will be with you all the time.

Membership costs thirty-two pounds a month for adults, and students and people over sixty-five pay twenty pounds. And if you join before the opening day, your first month is completely free.

We've also got something special on Sunday mornings. The pool will be open only for parents and children, and there'll be games and floating toys in the water.

Lots of people have asked us about getting here. There is a car park, but it only has forty spaces, so we'd really recommend coming by bike. We've put a large bike shelter right next to the main entrance. The number fourteen bus stops outside too, but it only runs once an hour.

Finally, if you'd like to look around before you join, we're running free tours every afternoon this week. They leave from the reception desk at four o'clock, and they take about half an hour. I hope to see lots of you there.

horenParts.instruction: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
horenParts.transcript:
Interviewer: My guest today is Leila Ahmed, who designs video games. Leila, how did you first get interested in making games?
Leila: People often think I had a teacher who pushed me, but actually my teachers thought games were a complete waste of time. And I certainly didn't expect to get rich! What happened was that as a teenager I used to change the levels in the games I'd bought. I'd add new rooms, make the monsters harder, that kind of thing. I enjoyed that far more than just playing them.
Interviewer: And then you went to university?
Leila: Yes, I studied games design. The programming was hard, and at one point I thought about switching to an art course, but I'm glad I didn't. Looking back, the most useful thing was the group projects. In this industry nobody works alone, and that's where I learnt to listen to other people's ideas and share my own.
Interviewer: What was your first job like?
Leila: It was at a small company in Manchester. I'd imagined I'd spend my days inventing characters, but in fact I spent most of my time playing the same level again and again to find mistakes. I had no idea how much testing goes into a game. It wasn't boring exactly, it taught me to be patient, and my boss was very kind to me. I just hadn't expected it.
Interviewer: What do you think makes a really good game?
Leila: Well, everyone talks about the graphics, and of course a good story helps. But for me, if a player can't understand what to do in the first two minutes, they'll stop playing, however beautiful the game looks. So simple rules come first. Everything else is built on that.
Interviewer: Some parents worry that young people spend too much time on games. What's your view?
Leila: I don't think games are bad for young people at all. Lots of them teach you to solve problems. But I've got two children myself, and they have to go outside and see their friends as well. An hour or so after their homework seems about right to me. And I don't mind whether it's an educational game or not. To be honest, a lot of educational games aren't very good!
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to listeners who'd like to design games?
Leila: Don't wait. You don't have to go to university first, and you certainly don't need to start as a tester like I did. There are free programs that let you build a small game in a weekend. Make something simple, show it to your friends and listen carefully to what they say. That's how you learn.
Interviewer: Leila Ahmed, thank you very much.

schreibenParts.task:
Read this email from your English-speaking friend Sam and the notes you have made.

From: Sam
Subject: Maya's birthday

Hi!

It's Maya's birthday on the 18th and I'd love us to plan something special for her. [Note: Great idea!]

I was thinking of either a picnic in the park or going bowling. Which do you think she'd prefer? [Note: Say which and why]

I'd also like to buy her a present together with you. Have you got any ideas? [Note: Suggest...]

Could we meet this weekend to organise everything? [Note: Yes, tell Sam when]

Speak soon,
Sam

Write your email to Sam using all the notes. Write about 100 words.

Choose ONE of these questions. Write about 100 words.

Article
You see this notice on an English-language website for teenagers.

Articles wanted!
A celebration I will never forget
Tell us about a celebration you will always remember. What were you celebrating? Who was there? Why was it so special?
The best articles will appear on our website.

Write your article.

Story
Your English teacher has asked you to write a story. Your story must begin with this sentence:

Everyone shouted 'Surprise!' when I walked in.

Write your story.

sprechenParts.title: Part 1 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Answer the examiner's questions about yourself.

What's your name? Where do you live?
Do you work or are you a student?
What do you enjoy most about your studies or your job? Why?
How do you usually travel to your school, college or workplace?
Tell us about a teacher or a colleague who has helped you.
What would you like to study or do in the future?

sprechenParts.title: Part 2 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Look at the photograph. It shows a group of four young people working together at a large table in a bright office. One woman is pointing at a laptop screen, a man is writing notes on a whiteboard, and two others are looking at papers and smiling. There are coffee cups and coloured sticky notes on the table.

Tell us what you can see in the photograph. Talk for about one minute.

sprechenParts.title: Part 3 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
A group of students from your school has some free time on Saturday mornings and wants to do a short course together. Here are some courses they could choose:

a cooking course
a first aid course
a computer programming course
a photography course
a course in a foreign language
a course on how to start a small business

Talk together about the different courses the students could do, and say which would be the most useful for them. Then decide which course they should choose. Talk for about two or three minutes.

sprechenParts.title: Part 4 — Speaking
sprechenParts.situation:
Answer the examiner's questions and discuss them with your partner.

Do you prefer studying on your own or with other people? Why?
Is it a good idea for students to have a part-time job? Why or why not?
What skills do you think are most important for finding a good job today?
Would you like to work in an office, or somewhere else? Why?
Tell us about something new you have learnt recently. How did you learn it?
Do you think people will study more online in the future?
